items.stimulus:
In December 2012 Australia became the first country to require that cigarettes be sold in plain packaging. Under the new rules, logos, brand colours and promotional images disappeared from packs. Every pack had to be the same drab dark brown, a shade selected after consumer research found it the least appealing of the colours tested, and the brand name could appear only in a standard font, size and position. Graphic health warnings, which were already required, were enlarged to cover most of the front of the pack.

The reasoning behind the measure was that a pack is itself a form of advertising. Once television, print and sponsorship advertising of tobacco had been banned, the box carried in a pocket or left on a cafe table remained one of the few ways a brand could signal glamour, sophistication or rebellion, particularly to young people. Removing that signal, supporters argued, would make smoking less attractive to people who had not yet started, make the health warnings more noticeable, and stop design tricks such as pale colours from suggesting that some cigarettes were less harmful than others.

Tobacco companies responded with legal challenges. One argued before the High Court of Australia that stripping companies of the use of their trademarks amounted to taking their property without fair compensation; the court rejected the claim. Later challenges brought under an investment treaty and through the World Trade Organization also failed.

Judging whether the policy worked is harder than it might seem. Smoking rates in Australia were already falling before 2012, and tobacco taxes were raised repeatedly in the years around the change, so a decline afterwards cannot simply be credited to packaging. Researchers have therefore combined several kinds of evidence, including surveys of how appealing smokers found the new packs and statistical analyses that try to separate the effect of packaging from the effect of price. On balance, the fairest conclusion seems to be that plain packaging added modestly to a downward trend that was already under way rather than producing it on its own, and a modest contribution to reducing a leading cause of preventable death is still well worth having.

items.stimulus:
Most people believe that we owe something to those who will live after us: that it would be wrong, for example, to bury toxic waste in containers we know will start leaking in three hundred years. Yet philosophers have found this belief surprisingly hard to justify.

One difficulty concerns reciprocity. Many accounts of moral duty rest on the idea of cooperation between people who can benefit and burden one another. Future people cannot repay us, complain to us or hold us to account, so theories built on mutual exchange struggle to explain why we should owe them anything at all.

A second, stranger difficulty concerns identity. Exactly which people will exist in two centuries depends on countless choices made today, down to when couples meet and when children are conceived. Suppose a country adopts an energy policy that brings cheap power now but damages the environment later. Over decades, that choice will change where people live and work, and therefore who meets whom, so the individuals born under it will be different individuals from those who would have been born under a more cautious alternative. If their lives are still worth living, it seems they cannot complain that the policy made them worse off, since without it they would never have existed. Harming someone normally means leaving that person worse off than they would otherwise have been, and here no such person can be found.

Few people accept that this puzzle permits recklessness. Some respond that wrongdoing need not involve harming any particular person: knowingly bringing about a worse state of the world than we could easily have avoided is wrong in itself. Others argue that we owe duties to whoever will occupy a future position, such as the residents of a particular valley in the year 2200, regardless of who those residents turn out to be. Neither answer has won general agreement, but both treat the conclusion that we may ignore the future as a sign that something in the original reasoning has gone wrong.

items.stimulus:
For most of history, concert halls that sounded good did so largely by luck. That began to change at the end of the nineteenth century, when Wallace Sabine, a young assistant professor of physics at Harvard University, was asked to improve a lecture room in which speech was almost impossible to follow. Working at night with organ pipes and a stopwatch, and carrying seat cushions in and out of the room, he measured how long a sound took to die away and found a simple relationship: the reverberation time of a room rises as its volume increases and falls as the amount of sound-absorbing material inside it increases. Boston's Symphony Hall, which opened in 1900, was the first concert hall designed with his findings in mind, and it is still admired.

Reverberation is not the enemy. A hall with too little of it makes an orchestra sound dry and thin, while one with too much blurs fast passages into a wash of sound. For symphonic music, designers usually aim for a reverberation time of around two seconds when the hall is full; speech needs far less. Because people absorb sound, the audience is part of the acoustic design. Seats are therefore often upholstered so that an empty seat absorbs about as much sound as an occupied one, which allows a rehearsal in an empty hall to sound similar to a performance.

Shape also matters. Tall, narrow rectangular halls, often called shoeboxes, send early reflections towards listeners from the side walls, and listeners tend to hear such sideways reflections as giving the music a pleasing sense of spaciousness. In the 1960s the Philharmonie in Berlin broke with this tradition by surrounding the orchestra with terraces of seating, an arrangement known as a vineyard. Its designers used the low walls between the terraces to recreate the side reflections that a shoebox provides naturally, and the vineyard plan has since been widely copied.

During the 1930s a stretch of the southern Great Plains of the United States, centred on the panhandles of Oklahoma and Texas, became known as the Dust Bowl. Severe drought was the immediate trigger, but the disaster had deeper roots. In the preceding decades, encouraged by high wheat prices during the First World War and by tractors that made large-scale cultivation cheaper, farmers had ploughed up millions of acres of native grassland. The federal government responded with new agencies and programmes. A Soil Conservation Service was created in 1935 to teach farmers, and pay them, to adopt methods such as contour ploughing, crop rotation and returning fields to grass, and millions of trees were planted in long windbreaks across the region. When the rains returned at the end of the decade, these practices helped the land to recover, although later droughts showed that the plains remained vulnerable.

items.stimulus:
Modern agriculture relies on a fairly narrow range of crop varieties, chosen for high yields and uniformity. Yet the older local varieties they have replaced, along with the wild relatives of crops, carry genes that may one day be needed to breed resistance to a new disease or tolerance of heat and drought. Seed banks exist to keep that genetic diversity available.

Most seeds can be stored by drying them to a low moisture content and keeping them cold, often at about minus 18 degrees Celsius. Under these conditions many will remain alive for decades. They do not last indefinitely, however, so a well-run bank must periodically test whether its samples still germinate and, when viability falls, grow the plants out to produce fresh seed. This regeneration is slow and expensive, and in poorly funded collections it is often the first task to be neglected.

The best-known facility, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008 inside a mountain on a Norwegian Arctic island. It is designed as a backup rather than a working collection: national and international seed banks send it duplicate samples, which remain their property and can be withdrawn only by the bank that deposited them. The first withdrawal came in 2015, when a research centre forced out of Aleppo by the war in Syria asked for copies of seeds it had deposited, so that it could rebuild its collection elsewhere.

Seed banks have limits. The seeds of some important plants, including cocoa and many tropical fruit trees, die if they are dried, so they must be kept as living plants in field collections or by more specialised methods. And seeds in storage are frozen in time: they do not continue to adapt as climates and pests change. For this reason, conservation in farmers' fields, where traditional varieties are grown and selected year after year, is best seen as a partner to seed banks rather than a rival. A seed bank can preserve what exists; only continued cultivation allows a variety to keep evolving.

items.stimulus:
In 1986, to mark nine hundred years since William the Conqueror's great survey of England, the BBC produced a modern equivalent: a multimedia record of life in Britain, contributed by around a million people, including many schoolchildren, and stored on special laser discs that could be read only by a particular computer and disc player. Within about fifteen years the equipment had become so rare that the record was in danger of becoming unreadable, while the original survey, written on parchment in the eleventh century, could still be consulted in an archive.

The episode is often cited to show that digital information is more fragile than it looks. Two distinct problems are involved. The first is physical: magnetic tapes, discs and flash memory degrade, and even when the medium survives, the machines needed to read it may not. The second is logical: a file is only a sequence of numbers, and it has meaning only to software that knows how to interpret its format. When that software is no longer available, or no longer runs on current computers, the data may survive perfectly yet be impossible to understand.

Archivists use two main strategies against the second problem. Migration converts files into newer formats before the old ones become unreadable, but each conversion risks losing features such as page layout, embedded fonts or the behaviour of interactive elements. Emulation instead leaves the original files unchanged and runs new software that imitates the old computer, so that the original programs can open the files as they once did. Emulation preserves the original experience more faithfully, but it depends on someone continuing to maintain the emulators themselves.

Neither strategy works without planning. Archives increasingly prefer formats whose specifications are openly published, keep several copies in different places, and check those copies regularly for silent corruption. The lesson of the laser discs is not that digital storage is hopeless, but that, unlike parchment, it cannot simply be left on a shelf.

items.stimulus:
A cooperative is a business owned and democratically controlled by the people it serves or employs rather than by outside investors. In a consumer cooperative, such as a food shop or a mutual insurer, the owners are its customers; in a worker cooperative, they are its employees. The usual rule is one member, one vote, however much capital each member has put in, and any surplus is returned to members according to how much they have used the business or worked in it, not according to how much they have invested.

The modern movement is often traced to a group of weavers and other workers in Rochdale, in the north of England, who in 1844 opened a shop selling basic goods at fair prices and drew up rules for running it democratically. Many of those rules still shape cooperatives today. Among worker cooperatives, a frequently discussed example is a large group of firms founded in the Basque Country of Spain in the 1950s, which now employs tens of thousands of people in manufacturing, retail and finance.

Supporters argue that cooperatives keep wealth within local communities and give people a say in decisions that affect their livelihoods. Some studies suggest that, when trade falls, worker cooperatives are more likely than conventional firms to cut hours or pay across the board rather than dismiss staff, so that employment is more stable even if incomes fluctuate.

The model also faces persistent difficulties. Because outside investors cannot buy control, cooperatives can find it hard to raise large amounts of capital quickly. Democratic decision-making can become slow as membership grows. And successful worker cooperatives sometimes take on many employees who are not members, gradually coming to resemble the conventional firms they set out to offer an alternative to. None of these problems is unique to cooperatives, but together they help to explain why the model, though widespread, has not displaced the investor-owned company as the dominant form of enterprise.

In a series of experiments that began in the late 1960s, researchers at Stanford University offered preschool children a choice: eat one treat, such as a marshmallow, straight away, or wait alone in a room for a set period, often around a quarter of an hour, and then receive two. Some children ate the treat almost at once; others distracted themselves by singing, covering their eyes or turning away from it. The original aim was to understand the strategies children use to resist temptation.

The studies became famous for a later finding. When the researchers followed up some of the original participants years afterwards, those who had waited longer as preschoolers tended, on average, to have higher scores on a university entrance test and were rated by their parents as better able to cope with stress. The idea that a few minutes in front of a marshmallow could predict later success proved irresistible to popular writers.

More recent work has complicated this picture. The original children came mostly from families connected with the university, and the follow-up samples were small. A larger study published in 2018, using a more varied group of children, found that the link between waiting time and later achievement was considerably weaker than in the original reports, and that it shrank further once the researchers took account of factors such as family income and the children's early language and thinking skills. Another experiment found that children who had just seen an adult break a promise waited much less time than children whose adult had kept their word, suggesting that waiting may partly reflect a sensible judgement about whether the second treat will ever arrive.

None of this shows that self-control is unimportant. It does suggest that a child's behaviour in a single short test reflects circumstances as well as character, and that the test is a poor tool for predicting any individual child's future.

items.stimulus:
The common octopus has around five hundred million neurons, but the way those neurons are arranged is very different from the arrangement in a vertebrate. Roughly two-thirds of them lie not in the brain but in the eight arms, each of which contains its own chain of nerve clusters running along its length. An arm can therefore carry out complex movements, such as reaching towards an object and bending to grasp it, with only general direction from the brain. Experiments have shown that an arm separated from the body may continue for a time to respond to touch and to grip objects.

The suckers add another layer of local processing. They carry large numbers of chemical receptors, allowing an octopus, in effect, to taste what it touches. An arm exploring a crevice can detect prey and begin to act on that information before the central brain has necessarily registered it.

Octopuses are capable of feats usually associated with vertebrates. Captive animals have learned to unscrew lids, escaped from their tanks and distinguished between individual human keepers. In the wild, some carry empty shells or coconut halves to use later as shelters. What makes this remarkable is their ancestry. Octopuses are molluscs, related to snails and clams, and their last common ancestor with humans was a simple creature that lived more than five hundred million years ago. Whatever intelligence octopuses possess therefore evolved separately from our own.

Their lives are also short. Most octopus species live for only a year or two, and females typically die soon after their eggs hatch, so young octopuses have little opportunity to learn from their parents. Much of what an octopus knows, it must work out for itself. For researchers, the animal offers a rare chance to study how a complex mind might be built on an entirely different plan from that of a vertebrate brain.

items.stimulus:
Countries take two broad approaches to consent for organ donation after death. Under an opt-in system, used in Australia among other places, a person becomes a donor only if they or their family actively agree. Under an opt-out system, sometimes called deemed or presumed consent, adults are treated as willing donors unless they have recorded an objection. Spain, which has had an opt-out law since 1979, has for many years reported one of the highest rates of deceased donation in the world, and Wales, England and Scotland have all moved to opt-out systems since 2015.

The appeal of opt-out is easy to see. Surveys in many countries find that far more people say they support donation than have formally registered as donors, and a default that matches most people's stated wishes seems likely to close that gap. Behavioural research also shows that people tend to stay with whatever option is presented to them as the default.

The evidence is less straightforward than this suggests, however. Spain's donation rate did not rise sharply until about a decade after its law was passed, when the country created a national transplant organisation and placed trained donation coordinators in its hospitals. Many specialists therefore credit Spain's results mainly to this organisational model rather than to the law itself. In practice, most opt-out systems are soft: families are still consulted, and doctors rarely proceed if relatives object. Since families can also refuse in opt-in systems, the real difference between the two may lie less in who has the final say than in how the conversation with the family begins.

Another constraint applies whatever the law. Only a very small proportion of people die in circumstances that allow their organs to be used, usually in an intensive care unit after a severe brain injury, so the number of potential donors is limited before consent is even discussed. Changing the default may help families feel confident that donation is what their relative would have wanted, and that is valuable. But a country hoping for a large increase in transplants will probably need to invest in hospital systems, staff training and public conversation as well as, or instead of, changing its consent law.
